summary: This paper proposes embedding a SNAIL amplifier on-chip within the readout chain of superconducting qubits to enable coherent, directional signal processing and parametric amplification, replacing bulky external isolators and achieving higher readout fidelity through a "Catch-Process-Release" protocol. The architecture uses frequency-multiplexed parametric interactions to sequentially squeeze, displace, convert, and amplify the readout signal while it remains in the high-Q readout and SNAIL resonators, then releases it to a fast output resonator for extraction.
motivation: Conventional dispersive readout requires external circulators and isolators that introduce losses, thermal load, and hardware overhead, while limiting information efficiency by forcing continuous signal extraction. Integrating on-chip directional amplification could eliminate these bottlenecks and enable scalable readout with reduced photon budgets.
method: A readout resonator (dispersively coupled to a qubit), SNAIL mode, and output resonator are weakly hybridized at detuned frequencies. Parametric pumps at sum/difference frequencies activate three-wave mixing processes (squeezing, beam-splitter conversion, phase-sensitive amplification) via the cubic SNAIL nonlinearity, implemented as a five-gate sequence: readout squeezing, displacement under dispersive rotation, readout-to-SNAIL conversion, phase-sensitive amplification, and SNAIL-to-output conversion. System dynamics are modeled using covariance-matrix descriptions of linear, time-varying Gaussian systems.
result: The Embedded Amplifier protocol achieves 99.9% fidelity with $\sim 5$ photons and $\sim 1$ µs integration time, compared to Conventional Dispersive Readout requiring significantly longer times or higher photon budgets; the narrow dead-time overhead ($\sim 300$ ns) of parametric gate operations is offset by the ability to saturate SNR at optimal interaction time $t_a = \pi/2\chi$ ($\chi \approx 3$ MHz), and efficiency approaches unity by eliminating losses from external components and implementing on-chip quantum-limited amplification.
